d11c1d7de25c3596.text: Your payslip is a text. Every job comes with a payslip. It might be paper, an email or a page in an app. It's easy to ignore. Don't. A payslip is a text, just like a news article or an ad. It has a purpose: to show what you earned and how it was worked out. It has an audience: you (and the tax office). And it has a structure that's nearly the same everywhere. Read it from top to bottom: Who and when — your employer's name and ABN, your name, the pay period (the days it covers) and the pay date. Earnings — your hours, your rate per hour, and the amount. Weekend or late hours may have a higher penalty rate. Gross pay — the total before anything is taken out. Deductions — usually tax withheld, which your employer sends to the ATO for you. Net pay — what actually goes into your bank. Super — extra money your employer pays into your super fund. From 1 July 2025 it's 12% of your ordinary earnings. By law, you must get a payslip within one working day of payday. If something looks wrong, check your own record of your hours first. Then ask your manager — politely and in writing, so there's a record. If that doesn't fix it, the Fair Work Ombudsman can help.

63b51fe7d2b4e379.text: $358 million paid back. The Fair Work Ombudsman is a government body. Its job is to check that workers are paid properly. In 2024–25, it got back $358 million for workers who were paid too little. That money went to more than 249,000 people. It also said young workers aged 15 to 24 made more than their share of anonymous reports. Many young people work casual jobs. Many don't know their rights, or don't read their payslips closely. Most of that money came back because someone noticed a problem and spoke up. Think about it. Who is the Fair Work Ombudsman, and what does it do? Why might young workers be more likely to be underpaid? What's one thing on a payslip you could check to spot underpayment?

77dd2de373eeb20e.text: Super just went up. Super is money your employer must pay into a super fund for you, on top of your wages. It's for retirement — but it's legally your money. The ATO told employers that from 1 July 2025 the super guarantee rate rose to 12% of your ordinary time earnings, applying to all wages paid from that date. If you earn $500 in ordinary pay, your employer pays another $60 into your super. One catch: if you're under 18, your employer only has to pay super for weeks when you work more than 30 hours. Your payslip should show super paid and the fund name — and it's worth checking your fund to make sure it actually arrived. Think about it. How much super would you get on $200 of ordinary pay?
